title: Memory & Performance
intro: Memory leaks, GC pauses and a blocked event loop are the most common reasons a Node.js service falls over in production. Interviewers ask about them to see whether you can reason about what V8 is doing and debug with real tools instead of guessing. A senior answer explains the mechanism in plain words, names the exact flags and APIs, and always starts with measuring.

questions.title: Stack vs heap, V8 heap layout
questions.question: Where do values live in memory in a Node.js process? Explain the stack, the heap, and how V8 splits the heap.
questions.short: The stack holds call frames: local variables, arguments and return addresses for the function currently running. It is small and freed automatically when a function returns. Objects, arrays, closures and strings live on the heap, which the garbage collector manages. V8 splits the heap into a young generation (new space), where new objects are allocated and most die quickly, and an old generation (old space), where objects that survive a couple of collections are promoted. There are also special spaces such as large object space and code space, and Buffer data usually lives outside the V8 heap entirely.
questions.simple: The stack is a stack of sticky notes for the function you are in right now; you throw the top note away when the function ends. The heap is a big warehouse for everything that needs to stay around, and a cleaner (the garbage collector) walks it to throw away boxes nobody points to.

explain.p: When a function runs, V8 pushes a frame on the stack. Small values like numbers that fit in a "Smi" (small integer) can sit directly in the frame, but anything like `{}`, `[]`, a closure or most strings is allocated on the heap, and the frame only holds a pointer to it.

head: Area
What lives there
Freed by
rows: freed when the JS wrapper is collected

explain.p: The young generation is small (a few MB to tens of MB, tunable with `--max-semi-space-size`). The old generation is large and is what `--max-old-space-size` limits.

explain.note: A "stack overflow" (RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded) is about recursion depth, not about heap size. "JavaScript heap out of memory" is about the heap. Interviewers like to check you do not mix them up.

explain.p: You can inspect the spaces with `v8.getHeapSpaceStatistics()`, which lists `new_space`, `old_space`, `code_space`, `large_object_space` and others with their sizes.

anim.title: Where things go

steps.note: The module creates a Map. It is referenced by a module-level variable, which is reachable from the roots.
Calling handle(1) pushes a new frame. id=1 is a small integer, stored right in the frame.
The object and its array are allocated in new space. The frame only holds a pointer.
JSON.stringify creates a string, also on the heap in new space.
Storing user in the Map makes it reachable from a root, even after the function returns.
handle returns. Its frame is popped instantly; that is the stack "freeing" memory with zero GC work.
A scavenge runs. tmp is unreachable, so it is simply not copied and its space is reused.
After surviving another scavenge, the long-lived Map, user and tags are promoted to old space.

followups.q: Are strings on the stack?
followups.a: No. Strings are heap objects in V8. Only small integers (Smis) and pointers are stored directly in frames or object fields.

followups.q: How big is the default stack?
followups.a: Around 1 MB on 64-bit systems (V8 flag --stack-size, in KB). You hit its limit through deep recursion, not by allocating big objects.

mistakes: Saying "primitives go on the stack, objects on the heap" as a hard rule. In V8 most strings and doubles in objects are heap values too.
Confusing a stack overflow with running out of heap.
Forgetting that Buffer memory is mostly outside the V8 heap.

questions.title: How garbage collection works
questions.question: How does garbage collection work in V8? Explain scavenge, mark-sweep-compact, and the generational idea in plain words.
questions.short: V8 uses a generational collector based on the idea that most objects die young. New objects go into the small young generation, which is cleaned by a fast Scavenge: live objects are copied to the other half of the space and everything left behind is garbage. Objects that survive two scavenges are promoted to the old generation, which is cleaned less often by Mark-Sweep-Compact: mark everything reachable from roots, sweep the rest, and compact to reduce fragmentation. Most of this work runs concurrently or incrementally on helper threads, but some phases still pause JavaScript.
questions.simple: Think of a cafe. The trays on the counter (young generation) are cleared constantly because most people leave fast. Customers who stay a long time move to the back room (old generation), which is only cleaned in a big sweep every now and then.

explain.p: GC never asks "is this used?". It asks "can I reach this from a root?". Roots include global objects, the current call stack, and handles held by native code. Anything not reachable is garbage, even if you think of it as "in use". Anything reachable stays, even if you never touch it again, which is how leaks happen.

The young generation has two halves (semi-spaces). Allocation fills one half. When it is full, V8 copies the live objects to the other half and the old half is treated as empty. The cost depends on how many objects are alive, not on how much garbage there is, which is why short-lived garbage is cheap. V8 runs this in parallel on several threads.

list: Mark: starting from roots, follow every pointer and mark what is reachable. Done mostly concurrently and incrementally while JS runs.
Sweep: free the memory of unmarked objects, done concurrently on helper threads.
Compact: move surviving objects together in fragmented pages so memory is contiguous again. Only some pages are compacted.

head: Scavenge
Mark-Sweep-Compact
rows: longer, mostly hidden by concurrent work

explain.note: Signs of GC trouble: rising p99 latency and high CPU without more traffic. Run with `--trace-gc` to log every GC with its pause time, or look at the GC entries in a CPU profile.

explain.p: Practical advice: avoid keeping lots of medium-lived objects (they survive scavenges, get promoted, then die in old space, the most expensive pattern). Reuse buffers in hot paths and avoid building huge temporary arrays.

anim.title: Generational GC in action

steps.note: The sessions Map is created and referenced from module scope, so it is reachable from a root.
A request comes in. The parsed body is a temporary object in new space.
A session object is created and stored in the Map, so it is reachable.
render creates more temporary objects. After the function returns, body1 and html1 are unreachable.
More requests fill new space with mostly temporary data.
New space is full, so a Scavenge runs. It copies only live objects (Map, s1, s2) to the other semi-space.
Garbage was never touched, just left behind. That is why short-lived objects are almost free.
After surviving a second scavenge, the Map and sessions are promoted to old space.
Later, s1 is deleted from the Map. It sits in old space, unreachable, until a major GC.
Mark phase: walk from roots. Map and s2 are marked; s1 is not. Mostly done concurrently while JS runs.
Sweep frees s1. Compaction may move survivors together to reduce fragmentation.

followups.q: Does V8 use reference counting?
followups.a: No. It uses tracing (reachability from roots), so cycles of objects that point to each other but are unreachable from roots are collected fine.

followups.q: Can you trigger GC manually?
followups.a: Only with the --expose-gc flag, which exposes global.gc(). It is useful in tests and leak experiments, but calling it in production usually hurts performance.

followups.q: What is a "stop-the-world" pause?
followups.a: A moment where JS execution is paused so the GC can safely work. Modern V8 keeps these short by doing most marking and sweeping concurrently, but large live heaps still mean longer pauses.

mistakes: Saying "setting a variable to null frees memory". It only removes one reference; the object is freed at the next GC if nothing else points to it.
Believing circular references leak in V8.
Assuming GC cost depends on the amount of garbage; for scavenges it depends on the amount of live data.

questions.title: --max-old-space-size and containers
questions.question: What does --max-old-space-size do, and how should you set Node.js memory limits when running in a container with, say, 1 GB of RAM?
questions.short: --max-old-space-size sets the maximum size of V8's old generation in megabytes. When the old space cannot grow past it, V8 does a last-ditch GC and then crashes with "JavaScript heap out of memory". It does not cover the young generation, Buffers, native memory or the code itself, so in a 1 GB container you set it to about 70-80% of the limit, for example 768, to leave headroom for everything else. Newer Node versions read the cgroup limit and size the heap from it, but setting it explicitly is still the safest choice.
questions.simple: It is the size of the big storage room for long-lived objects. The whole house (container) must also fit the hallway, the garage (Buffers) and the furniture (native code), so the storage room cannot be as big as the whole house.

explain.code:
node --max-old-space-size=768 server.js

# or via env, handy in Dockerfiles and Kubernetes
NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=768" node server.js

list: As the old space approaches the limit, V8 runs GC more and more often. CPU goes up and latency gets worse before the crash.
If a major GC still cannot free enough, the process aborts with "FATAL ERROR: ... JavaScript heap out of memory".
If instead the total process memory (RSS) crosses the container limit first, the kernel OOM-killer sends SIGKILL. You see exit code 137 and no JavaScript stack trace.

head: Symptom
Likely cause
rows: "JavaScript heap out of memory" in logs
RSS hit the container limit (heap too big, or lots of Buffers/native memory)
High CPU, many GC lines with --trace-gc

explain.p: Check what V8 actually picked with `v8.getHeapStatistics().heap_size_limit`. Log it at startup so you can see the effective limit in every environment.

explain.note: Raising the heap limit does not fix a leak; it just delays the crash and makes each major GC slower. Raise it only when the workload genuinely needs more live data.

explain.p: Also consider `--max-semi-space-size` (young generation size, in MB). A bigger young generation can reduce scavenge frequency and promotions for allocation-heavy services, at the cost of more memory.

followups.q: Does --max-old-space-size limit Buffer memory?
followups.a: No. Buffer contents are allocated outside the V8 heap, so they count toward RSS and the container limit but not toward the old space limit.

followups.q: How do you get a heap snapshot at the moment of an OOM?
followups.a: Use --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=N, which writes up to N snapshots when the heap is close to the limit, or --diagnostic-dir to choose where they go.

mistakes: Setting --max-old-space-size equal to the container memory limit, leaving no room for Buffers and native memory.
Treating a higher heap limit as a leak fix.
Not recognizing exit code 137 as an external OOM kill rather than a V8 heap error.

questions.title: process.memoryUsage() fields
questions.question: What do the fields of process.memoryUsage() mean, and which ones would you alert on?
questions.short: rss is the total memory the OS has given the process: heap, stack, code, native allocations and Buffers. heapTotal is how much V8 has reserved for the JS heap, and heapUsed is how much of that is actually holding objects. external is memory for C++ objects bound to JS objects, including Buffer contents, and arrayBuffers is the part of external used by ArrayBuffers and Buffers. I would graph heapUsed after GC to spot leaks, and alert on rss against the container limit, because that is what the OOM-killer uses.
questions.simple: rss is the size of your whole apartment. heapTotal is the size of the living room, heapUsed is how much of the living room is full of furniture, and external is the stuff stored in the garage (Buffers).

head: Field
Meaning
Watch for
rows: resident set size: all memory in RAM for the process
sawtooth whose low points keep rising = leak
memory of C++ objects tied to JS, incl. Buffers

explain.p: heapUsed naturally goes up and down in a sawtooth: it climbs as you allocate and drops after each GC. A leak shows up as the bottom of each tooth getting higher over hours or days.

explain.caption: Export memory metrics

explain.note: `process.memoryUsage()` iterates over V8's heap pages to gather its numbers, which can be slow-ish. For frequent sampling of just rss, use `process.memoryUsage.rss()`, which is cheaper.

explain.p: If rss is much bigger than heapTotal + external, suspect native memory: native addons, many threads, or allocator fragmentation (glibc malloc arenas). If external is big, look at Buffers being held (for example, cached file contents or buffered request bodies).

anim.title: Heap vs Buffer memory

steps.note: We take a baseline reading. A fresh process has a small heap and little external memory.
Buffer.alloc(50 MB): only a tiny JS wrapper goes on the heap. The 50 MB of bytes live off-heap.
A million small objects are real JS heap objects. Many survive scavenges and get promoted to old space.
Second reading. We compare the growth of each field.
external grew by about 50 MB because Buffer bytes count there, not in the heap.
arrayBuffers is the Buffer/ArrayBuffer part of external, so it grew the same way.
heapUsed grew because of the million objects, not because of the Buffer.
rss covers everything resident: heap, external, code and stacks. In practice it is larger than heapTotal.
We use both values at the end so they stay reachable during the measurement.

followups.q: Why can rss stay high after a big spike even though heapUsed dropped?
followups.a: V8 and the system allocator do not always return freed pages to the OS right away. rss may stay elevated until memory pressure or later compaction. It is not necessarily a leak.

followups.q: Where else can you see heap details?
followups.a: v8.getHeapStatistics() for totals and the heap limit, and v8.getHeapSpaceStatistics() for each space (new, old, code, large object).

mistakes: Alerting on heapUsed peaks, which are normal before a GC.
Expecting Buffers to show up in heapUsed.
Thinking rss equals heapTotal.

questions.title: Common memory leak sources
questions.question: What are the most common causes of memory leaks in Node.js applications?
questions.short: A leak in a GC language means something keeps a reference to objects you no longer need, so they stay reachable. The usual suspects are: unbounded in-process caches or Maps keyed by request or user ID; event listeners added per request and never removed; setInterval or timers that capture large objects and are never cleared; closures that hold on to big objects longer than needed; and unbounded queues or arrays when producers are faster than consumers. Global variables, including accidental ones, make all of these worse.
questions.simple: GC only throws away things nobody is pointing at. A leak is like keeping every receipt "just in case" in a drawer you never empty: each one is small, but the drawer is always reachable and never cleaned.

head: Source
Example
Fix
rows: LRU with max size and TTL
emitter.on('data', h) inside a request handler
callback keeps a reference to a whole request/response
copy just the fields you need
awaiting a promise that never resolves holds its closure

explain.caption: Each disconnected client leaves a listener (and its res) alive

explain.p: The leaked listener keeps `onPrice` alive, which keeps `res` alive through the closure, which keeps the socket, buffers and request objects alive. A small leak per request can hold megabytes.

explain.note: Node prints "MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 update listeners added" when an emitter gets more than 10 listeners for one event. Do not just raise setMaxListeners; check whether listeners are being removed.

list: Module-level arrays used for "debugging" or metrics (`const seen = []`) grow forever.
Memoize helpers without limits (e.g. caching every distinct input) are caches too.
Logging libraries or APM agents misconfigured to buffer when the sink is down.

anim.title: A listener leak, request by request

steps.note: A module-level emitter is reachable from the roots for the life of the process.
Client 1 connects. A closure is added as a listener; it captures res1.
Clients 2 and 3 connect. Each adds its own listener and closure.
Client 1 disconnects. Nobody removes onPrice1, so prices -> onPrice1 -> res1 stays reachable.
GC runs. It walks from roots, reaches every listener, and frees nothing. GC cannot know res1 is "dead".
After thousands of reconnects, old space is full of dead responses and the warning appears.
Fix: on 'close', call prices.off('update', onPrice). The chain from the root is cut, so the next GC frees it.

followups.q: How can AbortSignal help with listener cleanup?
followups.a: events.on(emitter, name, { signal }) and EventTarget's addEventListener(type, fn, { signal }) accept an AbortSignal; aborting it removes the listener, so you can tie cleanup to a request's lifetime. For a plain emitter.on(), call emitter.off() in the request's close handler.

followups.q: Is a cache a leak?
followups.a: Only if it is unbounded. A cache with a size limit and eviction has a fixed maximum memory cost, which is a design decision, not a leak.

mistakes: Raising setMaxListeners to silence the warning instead of fixing the missing cleanup.
Using a plain object or Map as a cache with no eviction.
Assuming a closure only keeps the variables it uses; in V8, closures created in the same scope share one context, so a variable used by any of them stays alive as long as any of them is alive.

questions.title: Debugging a leak in production
questions.question: Memory in your Node.js service grows slowly until it restarts every day. How do you find the leak?
questions.short: First confirm it is a leak: graph heapUsed after GC and rss over time, and correlate with traffic and deploys. Then reproduce in staging if possible and take heap snapshots: one at baseline, one after load, one after more load. Load them in Chrome DevTools, use the Comparison view to see which object types keep growing, and follow the Retainers path back to the root that holds them. In production, you can take snapshots with --heapsnapshot-signal, v8.writeHeapSnapshot(), or the inspector, remembering that a snapshot pauses the process and needs roughly as much extra memory as the heap.
questions.simple: Take three photos of the warehouse at different times. Whatever kind of box keeps piling up between the photos is your leak; then follow the label on the box to see who keeps ordering it.

list: Graph rss, heapUsed and external. A rising floor of heapUsed points to a JS leak; rising external points to Buffers; rising rss alone points to native memory.
Check if growth tracks traffic (per-request leak) or time (timer/interval leak).
Try --trace-gc to see whether major GCs reclaim less and less.

explain.code:
# Write a snapshot when the process receives SIGUSR2
node --heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2 server.js
kill -USR2 <pid>   # writes Heap.<date>.<pid>...heapsnapshot in cwd

# Automatically when close to the heap limit
node --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=2 server.js

# Attach Chrome DevTools (chrome://inspect) in staging
node --inspect=127.0.0.1:9229 server.js

list: Snapshot A after warm-up, B after N requests, C after another N requests.
In DevTools Memory tab, select C and choose Comparison against B (or "Objects allocated between A and B" in C).
Sort by "# Delta" or "Size Delta". Look for your own constructors, closures, arrays or strings growing by about N.
Click an instance and read the Retainers panel bottom-up: it shows the chain from a root (e.g. a module Map or an emitter listener array) to the object.

explain.note: Taking a heap snapshot is synchronous: the process freezes for seconds on a large heap and needs memory about the size of the heap to write it. Take it on one instance removed from the load balancer, never on all instances at once.

list: clinic.js (clinic doctor, clinic heapprofiler) to get a quick diagnosis and allocation flame graphs.
Allocation sampling (`--heap-prof` or the DevTools "Allocation sampling" profile) to see which functions allocate the most with low overhead.
APM tools that track heap and GC metrics per instance.

anim.title: Three snapshots, one suspect
anim.code:
# A: after warm-up
kill -USR2 $PID
# ...send 10,000 requests...
kill -USR2 $PID   # B
# ...send 10,000 more...
kill -USR2 $PID   # C
# DevTools: Comparison C vs B, then Retainers

steps.note: Snapshot A after warm-up. Caches are filled and lazy modules are loaded, so normal one-time growth is out of the picture.
After 10,000 requests, snapshot B. Most types are stable, but some grew.
After 10,000 more requests, snapshot C. Growth that repeats is the signal; one-time growth is noise.
The Comparison view shows Session grows by exactly one per request. Strings and Objects are flat.
Open one leaked Session and read its Retainers: it is held by a Map entry...
...and that Map is a module-level variable in auth.js that never deletes on logout or expiry. Root cause found.
After the fix, repeat the experiment. Session count should stay flat between B and C.

followups.q: What is the difference between shallow size and retained size?
followups.a: Shallow size is the memory of the object itself. Retained size is how much memory would be freed if that object were removed, including everything only it keeps alive. Sort by retained size to find what is holding the most.

followups.q: Is it safe to use --inspect in production?
followups.a: Only bound to localhost and reached through an SSH tunnel or kubectl port-forward. An exposed inspector port gives full remote code execution.

followups.q: How do you leak-test in CI?
followups.a: Run the scenario many times in a loop, force GC (--expose-gc), and assert heapUsed does not grow beyond a threshold.

mistakes: Taking only one snapshot; you need at least two (ideally three) to see what grows.
Taking snapshots on a production instance still serving traffic, causing a long freeze or OOM.
Exposing --inspect on 0.0.0.0.
Looking only at "(string)" or "Object" rows instead of your own constructors and the retainer chain.

questions.title: WeakMap and WeakRef for caches
questions.question: When would you use WeakMap or WeakRef? Can they replace a cache with a size limit?
questions.short: A WeakMap holds its keys weakly: if the key object is not reachable from anywhere else, the entry can be garbage collected. It is ideal for attaching metadata to objects you do not own, like caching derived data per request object, without extending their lifetime. A WeakRef lets you point at an object without keeping it alive, and deref() returns undefined after it is collected. Neither is a replacement for a real cache: you cannot control when GC happens, WeakMap keys must be objects and it cannot be iterated or sized, so for "keep the hottest 10,000 items" you still need an LRU with limits.
questions.simple: A WeakMap is a sticky note on someone else's box. When the box is thrown out, the note goes with it automatically. But you cannot count your notes or decide when boxes get thrown out.

head: Map
WeakMap
WeakRef
rows: no (key is weak; value lives while key lives)

explain.p: `FinalizationRegistry` lets you run a callback some time after an object is collected, for example to remove a dead WeakRef from a Map. The callback timing is not guaranteed and may never run, so never use it for important cleanup like closing files or releasing locks.

explain.note: The value in a WeakMap is held strongly as long as the key is alive. If the value references the key (value -> key), V8 still handles it correctly (ephemeron semantics), so it does not leak.

explain.p: Interview angle: "Can I fix my leaking cache by switching Map to WeakMap?" Usually no. If keys are strings like user IDs, WeakMap cannot even hold them. If keys are objects that stay alive elsewhere, nothing will be freed. Use a bounded LRU.

anim.title: A weak reference after GC

steps.note: Demo only: we enable --expose-gc at runtime so we can force a collection and see the effect deterministically.
user is a strong reference from a variable, so the object is reachable from the roots.
The WeakMap entry points from the object to its metadata. The key link is weak; it does not keep the object alive.
A WeakRef also points to the object weakly.
While the strong reference exists, both weak structures can see the object.
We drop the only strong reference. Only weak links remain, so the object is now collectable.
A WeakRef target is kept alive until the current job ends, so we wait one tick, then force GC.
GC freed the object and its WeakMap entry with it. deref() now returns undefined. In real life, you never know when this happens.

followups.q: Why can a WeakMap not be iterated?
followups.a: Its contents depend on when GC runs. Allowing iteration or size would make program behavior depend on GC timing, so the spec forbids it.

followups.q: What is a good use of WeakRef?
followups.a: A cache of large, re-creatable objects where it is fine to recompute if GC reclaimed them, often combined with FinalizationRegistry to clean up the Map entries holding the WeakRefs.

mistakes: Replacing a leaking Map<string, ...> cache with a WeakMap; string keys are not allowed.
Relying on FinalizationRegistry callbacks for essential cleanup.
Expecting a WeakRef to be cleared immediately after the last strong reference is dropped.

questions.title: In-process LRU cache with limits
questions.question: Implement a simple in-process LRU cache. How do you keep its memory bounded, and what are the trade-offs of caching inside the Node.js process?
questions.short: A JavaScript Map keeps insertion order, so an LRU is easy: on get, delete and re-insert the key to mark it most recent; on set, insert and, if over the limit, delete the first key, which is the least recently used. Both are O(1). Bound it by entry count and ideally by approximate byte size, and add a TTL so stale data expires. In-process caches are very fast but are per instance, lost on restart, add to heap size and GC work, and can return different data on different instances.
questions.simple: It is a short shelf by the door. When you use something, you put it at the front. When the shelf is full, the thing at the very back, the one nobody touched for the longest time, gets thrown out.

explain.caption: Minimal LRU using Map insertion order

list: Max entries and/or max bytes: track an approximate size per entry (e.g. Buffer.byteLength of a JSON string) and evict until under budget.
TTL: store expiresAt with each value; treat expired entries as misses and delete them.
Avoid thundering herd: when many requests miss the same key at once, store the in-flight promise so only one fetch happens.
Metrics: hit rate, evictions, size. A low hit rate means the cache is just extra memory.
In practice use a well-tested library such as lru-cache, which supports max, maxSize with sizeCalculation, and ttl.

explain.caption: Coalesce concurrent misses

head: In-process cache
Shared cache (e.g. Redis)
rows: per instance, can disagree between instances
uses your heap; big caches slow down GC

explain.note: A large cache of long-lived objects lives in old space, so every major GC has to mark it. A 1 GB in-process cache can noticeably increase GC pauses. Keep caches modest or store values as Buffers/strings to reduce object count.

anim.title: LRU with max = 2

steps.note: Create an LRU that keeps at most 2 entries. A Map remembers insertion order, so the first key is the oldest.
set('a', 1): the Map gets its first entry.
set('b', 2): b is the newest, a is now the oldest.
get('a'): it exists, so we delete it...
...and re-insert it. a moves to the newest end; b becomes the least recently used.
The value 1 is returned.
set('c', 3): inserted at the newest end. Size is now 3, over the limit.
keys().next() gives the first (oldest) key in O(1): b.
b is evicted. Memory stays bounded at 2 entries no matter how many keys we see.
get('b') is now a miss. The caller would fetch it from the source.
Final order: a (older), c (newest).

followups.q: What is wrong with checking `if (!this.map.get(key))` for a miss?
followups.a: Falsy values like 0, empty string or false would be treated as misses. Use has() or check for undefined explicitly.

followups.q: How would you invalidate entries across multiple instances?
followups.a: Use short TTLs, or publish invalidation messages (for example via Redis pub/sub) that each instance listens to and deletes the key locally.

mistakes: Building a cache with no max size or TTL, which is a memory leak by design.
Sorting by timestamps on every eviction (O(n log n)) instead of using Map order.
Caching huge objects in-process and then wondering why GC pauses grew.
Forgetting that each instance has its own cache and data can be inconsistent.

questions.title: CPU profiling and flame graphs
questions.question: Your Node.js service is using 100% CPU. How do you find out which code is responsible?
questions.short: Take a CPU profile. Node has a built-in sampling profiler: run with --cpu-prof to write a .cpuprofile file on exit, or attach Chrome DevTools via --inspect and record a profile under load. Open it as a flame graph: the x-axis is share of samples (time), the y-axis is call depth, and wide boxes at the top of a stack are the functions burning CPU themselves. Tools like 0x and clinic flame produce flame graphs directly. Look for hot functions, heavy JSON or regex work, and time spent in GC.
questions.simple: The profiler takes a photo of "what is the CPU doing right now" thousands of times a second. Functions that show up in the most photos are where the time goes.

explain.code:
# Built in: writes CPU.<date>.<pid>.cpuprofile on exit
node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=./profiles server.js
# generate load, then stop the process (Ctrl+C / SIGINT)
# open the file in Chrome DevTools > Performance, or in speedscope

# Flame graph tools
npx 0x server.js
npx clinic flame -- node server.js

# Linux perf (system-wide)
node --perf-basic-prof server.js

list: Each box is a function; the box below it is its caller.

Width = how many samples included that function = how much time. Order left-to-right is alphabetical or arbitrary, not time order. (Chrome DevTools' Performance "flame chart" is different: there the x-axis is time.)
Look for wide "plateaus" at the top: functions using CPU themselves (self time), not just calling others.
Look for (garbage collector) and (program) entries; a lot of GC time points to allocation pressure.

explain.p: Typical findings: a regex with catastrophic backtracking, `JSON.parse`/`stringify` of big payloads, synchronous crypto (`pbkdf2Sync`, `bcrypt` sync), sorting or deep-cloning large arrays on every request, or logging serializing huge objects.

explain.note: Sampling profilers have low overhead (a few percent), so a short profile on one production instance is often acceptable. Keep profiles short (30-60 seconds) under realistic load; profiling an idle process tells you nothing.

explain.p: You can also start and stop profiling programmatically with the `node:inspector` module (Session.post("Profiler.start") / "Profiler.stop"), for example behind an admin endpoint, to capture a profile only during the slow period.

anim.title: How a sampling profiler builds a flame graph

steps.note: Every ~1 ms the profiler interrupts and records the current stack. Sample 1 is inside loadData.
Sample 2 lands deep inside render -> slowFormat.
Samples 3 to 7 also land in slowFormat. It is clearly where time goes.
Samples 8 to 9 are in JSON.stringify.
One sample hits the garbage collector, which shows allocation pressure.
The flame graph stacks these: handler is ~90% wide (every sample except GC), render ~60%, slowFormat ~60% at the top. That wide top box is the target.
Fix slowFormat first (e.g. precompile the regex or simplify it). Optimizing loadData would barely matter.

followups.q: What is the difference between self time and total time?
followups.a: Self time is time spent in the function's own code. Total time also includes all functions it called. Hot spots to optimize usually have high self time.

followups.q: Why might a profile show little JS but CPU is still high?
followups.a: Time may be in native code, GC, or other threads (libuv thread pool for crypto/zlib). Check (garbage collector), (program), and use --trace-gc or OS tools like perf or top -H.

mistakes: Reading the x-axis of a flame graph as time order.
Profiling without load, or with unrealistic load.
Guessing and micro-optimizing before measuring.

questions.title: Finding a slow API endpoint
questions.question: One API endpoint got slow in production: p99 went from 80 ms to 900 ms. Walk me through how you would find the cause.
questions.short: First find out where the time goes: is the process slow for every request (event loop blocked, CPU, GC) or only this endpoint waiting on something (database, downstream API, pool)? I check per-endpoint latency metrics and traces to split the request into spans like DB, cache and external calls. I check event loop delay and CPU: if the loop is blocked, every endpoint suffers and a CPU profile finds the hot code. If only this endpoint is slow and the loop is healthy, it is usually I/O waiting: a slow query, missing index, connection pool exhaustion, or N+1 queries. Then I reproduce, fix, and confirm with the same metrics.
questions.simple: A slow pizza delivery can be a slow kitchen, a long queue for the one oven, or a traffic jam on the way. You time each part of the trip before you blame anyone.

head: Signal
Points to
rows: All endpoints slower, high event loop delay, CPU 100%
event loop blocked: sync CPU work, big JSON, GC
Only one endpoint slower, loop delay normal
awaited I/O: DB, HTTP calls, locks
Latency jumps under load, DB fast when tested alone
pool exhaustion: requests waiting for a connection
Many small DB queries per request in traces

explain.caption: Event loop delay is the first health check

list: Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) to see spans per request.
Per-route latency histograms (p50/p95/p99), not just averages.
Database slow query log and EXPLAIN for the queries this route runs.
Pool metrics: active, idle, waiting count.
clinic doctor to classify the issue (I/O, event loop, GC), then clinic flame or --cpu-prof for CPU.

explain.note: Check what changed: a deploy, a data growth threshold (a table that crossed millions of rows), a new client sending larger payloads, or a dependency upgrade. "What changed when it got slow" is often the fastest route.

explain.p: Measure in code with `performance.now()` around suspect steps, or use `AsyncLocalStorage` to attach a request ID to logs so you can follow one slow request end to end.

anim.title: Where did 900 ms go?

steps.note: The trace starts. auth takes 5 ms, which is normal.
Under load, all connections become busy. New requests queue for a connection before any SQL runs.
Our request waited 600 ms just for a connection. The query itself is not the main problem.
The query takes 250 ms because it scans a table that grew past a million rows without an index.
stringify of 5,000 orders takes 40 ms and blocks the event loop, which slows every other request too.
Root cause: the slow query holds connections longer, so the pool runs out and requests queue. Pool wait is the symptom.
Fix: add the index and paginate the response. Query drops to 5 ms, pool wait disappears, p99 recovers.

followups.q: Why look at p99 and not the average?
followups.a: Averages hide tail latency. A few very slow requests barely move the average but are what users notice and what causes timeouts upstream.

followups.q: Should you just increase the pool size?
followups.a: Only after fixing the slow query. A bigger pool can overload the database and make every query slower; the pool limit protects the DB.

mistakes: Jumping straight to code optimizations without measuring where time is spent.
Blaming Node when the time is spent waiting on the database.
Increasing pool size or timeouts to hide a slow query.

questions.title: Moving CPU work to worker_threads
questions.question: An endpoint does heavy CPU work (image resizing, big report generation, hashing) and blocks other requests. How do you fix it with worker_threads, and what are the trade-offs?
questions.short: Move the CPU-heavy function into a worker thread so the main event loop stays free to handle I/O. Each worker has its own V8 isolate and event loop, and you communicate with postMessage, which copies data using the structured clone algorithm, or transfers ArrayBuffers without copying. In production use a fixed-size pool of workers, roughly the number of CPU cores, with a queue in front, for example with Piscina, because starting a worker costs tens of milliseconds and memory. Workers help with CPU-bound work, not with I/O-bound work, which is already non-blocking.
questions.simple: The waiter (main thread) should not cook. When an order needs a lot of chopping, hand it to a cook in the kitchen (worker) and keep taking orders.

explain.caption: Minimal worker (eval: true only to keep the demo in one file)

list: Use a pool sized to available cores (`os.availableParallelism()`), not one worker per request.
Put a bounded queue in front of the pool; reject or shed load when it is full instead of buffering forever.
Use transferList for big binary data: `postMessage(buf.buffer, [buf.buffer])` moves ownership with no copy.
Handle `error` and `exit` events; restart crashed workers.
Set `resourceLimits` (for example maxOldGenerationSizeMb) so one job cannot eat all memory.

head: Option
Good for
Cost
rows: CPU work in the same process, shared memory possible
one isolate per worker (~ several MB), message copying
whole process per child, IPC is slower
does not unblock a slow request inside one worker
small CPU jobs, no extra threads
job itself still uses the main thread

explain.note: Copying a huge object to and from a worker can cost more than the work itself. Measure: if the job is 5 ms of CPU but serializing the input takes 20 ms, a worker makes things worse.

anim.title: Main thread stays free

steps.note: The main thread logs that the heavy job is starting.
new Worker starts a new thread with its own V8 isolate and event loop. Starting it takes some milliseconds.
A 0 ms timer is scheduled on the main thread. If we summed 10 million numbers here, this timer would be stuck.
The worker runs the loop in parallel on another core.
Meanwhile the main event loop is free, so the timer fires right away. This is what keeps other requests fast.
The worker finishes and posts the result. The number is copied to the main thread via structured clone.
The 'message' event resolves the promise, and the .then callback logs the sum.
The worker has no more work and nothing keeping its loop alive, so it exits, and then so does the process.

followups.q: Do worker threads share memory?
followups.a: Not by default; messages are copied. You can share memory explicitly with SharedArrayBuffer and coordinate with Atomics, or transfer ArrayBuffers to move ownership without copying.

followups.q: Would worker_threads help an endpoint that makes slow DB queries?
followups.a: No. Waiting on I/O does not block the event loop. Workers help only when JavaScript itself is burning CPU.

followups.q: How many workers should you create?
followups.a: Usually about the number of available cores minus one for the main thread, with a queue in front. More workers than cores just adds context switching.

mistakes: Spawning a new worker per request instead of using a pool.
Sending huge objects back and forth so that serialization costs more than the work.
Using workers for I/O-bound tasks.
Confusing worker_threads with cluster.

questions.title: Cost of JSON.parse / JSON.stringify
questions.question: Why can JSON.parse and JSON.stringify become a performance problem in Node.js, and what can you do about it?
questions.short: Both are synchronous and run on the main thread, and their cost grows with payload size. Parsing or stringifying a 50 MB payload can block the event loop for hundreds of milliseconds, during which no other request is served, and it creates a lot of garbage, which adds GC pressure. Fixes are to keep payloads small (pagination, field selection), use streaming parsers or NDJSON for large data, avoid stringifying the same object repeatedly (logging!), set body size limits, and move unavoidable large parsing to a worker thread.
questions.simple: JSON.parse is one cook reading a giant recipe book out loud; while they read, nobody else in the kitchen can be served.

list: Blocking: a single call cannot be interrupted, so its whole duration adds to every other request's latency.
Memory: the string, plus the parsed object graph (often several times larger than the text), exist at the same time.
GC pressure: millions of small objects are allocated, many promoted to old space, then freed.
Hidden costs: logging libraries that stringify full request/response objects, deep-cloning with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)).

explain.caption: Measure it on your own data shapes

list: Paginate and select only needed fields; most big-payload problems are API design problems.
For big exports, stream NDJSON (one JSON object per line) so each piece is parsed or stringified separately.
Use a streaming JSON parser for huge single documents you do not control.
Set request body size limits (e.g. express.json({ limit: "1mb" })) so one client cannot block the loop with a huge body.
Log only selected fields; use a fast structured logger (e.g. pino) and avoid serializing whole objects.
Use `structuredClone()` instead of the JSON round trip for deep copies; it supports more types (Date, Map, Set) but is still O(size).
For unavoidable big parses, offload to a worker thread, keeping in mind that passing the result back is also a copy.

explain.note: Schema-based serializers (like fast-json-stringify, used by Fastify) can be noticeably faster than JSON.stringify because they know the shape of the output in advance.

anim.title: A 50 MB parse blocks everyone

steps.note: A 50 MB import request arrives. The raw body string is already in memory.
JSON.parse starts. It is one synchronous call; the event loop cannot run anything else until it returns.
Health checks and other users' requests arrive, but they can only wait in the queue.
Millions of objects are created. Scavenges run inside the parse and promote most of them to old space.
After ~700 ms the parse finishes and the response is sent.
Only now can queued requests run. Each one got ~700 ms of extra latency; the load balancer health check may have timed out.
Fix: accept NDJSON and process it as a stream, line by line. Each JSON.parse is tiny, so other requests interleave.

followups.q: Is JSON.parse faster than a JavaScript object literal for big constant data?
followups.a: For large static data, V8 can parse JSON.parse('...') faster than an equivalent object literal, because the JSON grammar is simpler. This matters only for big embedded configs, not request handling.

followups.q: How do you protect against a client sending a 1 GB JSON body?
followups.a: Enforce a body size limit before parsing, check Content-Length early, and count bytes while streaming the body.

mistakes: Assuming JSON.parse is async or runs off the main thread.
Deep-cloning with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) in hot paths, which also loses Dates, Maps and undefined.
Logging entire request or response objects on every request.

questions.title: perf_hooks and event loop utilization
questions.question: How do you measure performance inside a Node.js app? Explain perf_hooks, event loop delay, and event loop utilization (ELU).
questions.short: node:perf_hooks gives high-resolution timing: performance.now(), marks and measures, PerformanceObserver to collect entries, timerify for functions, and histograms. For overall health, monitorEventLoopDelay measures how late timers fire, which tells you if the loop is blocked, and performance.eventLoopUtilization() reports the fraction of time the loop was busy versus idle waiting for I/O. ELU close to 1 means the process is CPU-saturated and adding traffic will only increase latency, which makes it a better scaling signal than CPU percent alone.
questions.simple: Event loop delay is "how late is the bus". Event loop utilization is "what share of the day was the driver actually driving, versus waiting at stops".

head: API
What it gives you
rows: monotonic high-resolution time in ms, for measuring durations
named timestamps and durations, visible to observers and tracing tools
callback receiving entries (measure, function, gc, http, dns...)
wraps fn so each call creates a "function" entry with its duration
histogram of event loop delay (min, max, mean, percentiles, in ns)
idle, active, utilization since start or since a previous reading
record your own values and get percentiles

explain.p: CPU percent counts all threads (GC helpers, libuv thread pool), and it can be misleading in containers. ELU measures only the main event loop: `active / (active + idle)`. A process with ELU 0.95 has almost no spare time to respond to new events, even if the machine CPU looks fine. Many teams autoscale or shed load on ELU.

explain.caption: Export ELU every 5 seconds

explain.note: Use `performance.now()` or `process.hrtime.bigint()` for durations, not `Date.now()`. Date.now has millisecond resolution and can jump when the system clock is adjusted.

explain.p: Worker threads have their own ELU (`worker.performance.eventLoopUtilization()`), which is useful for deciding if a worker pool is saturated.
Observer callbacks are delivered asynchronously in batches, not at the moment of the measure call. That is why, in the animation, "measured" prints before the observer's output.

anim.title: Measure, observe, and ELU

steps.note: An observer is registered for 'measure' entries. Its callback will run later, in a batch.
A timer is scheduled. The main script finishes and the event loop starts.
Inside the timer, we take an ELU reading as the starting point.
mark('start') records a named high-resolution timestamp.
busy(40) spins the CPU for 40 ms. The event loop is fully active and cannot do anything else.
mark('end') and measure() create a 'busy-loop' entry of about 40 ms.
measured prints first: the observer has not been called yet, because entries are delivered asynchronously.
A second timer is scheduled for 10 ms later. During that wait the loop is idle.
The observer callback runs with the batched entry. The duration is at least 30 ms.
The ELU check runs. Since elu1: about 40 ms active and about 10 ms idle.
Utilization is well above 0.5. In production, a sustained ELU near 1 means the instance is saturated.

followups.q: What is the difference between event loop delay and ELU?
followups.a: Delay tells you how late callbacks run (a symptom users feel). ELU tells you how busy the loop is overall (capacity). High ELU usually comes before high delay.

followups.q: How would you time a single function in production code?
followups.a: Use performance.timerify(fn) with a PerformanceObserver for "function" entries, or wrap the call with performance.now() and record the result in a histogram.

mistakes: Using Date.now() for fine-grained durations.
Watching only CPU percent and missing a saturated event loop.
Expecting PerformanceObserver callbacks to run synchronously at measure time.
